metadata.name: stat
metadata.displayName: stat - Display file or file system status
metadata.description: Display detailed file or file system status information

installation.note: stat is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: The stat command displays detailed information about files and file systems, including permissions, size, timestamps, inode number, and more. It's useful for debugging, scripting, and understanding file metadata.
when_to_use: View detailed file timestamps (access, modify, change)
Get file size and inode information

syntax.description: Display file status for one or more files. Can also display file system status with -f option.

options.description: Follow symbolic links and show information about the file they point to

options.description: Display file system status instead of file status
options.use_case: To check file system information like type, block size, and available space

options.use_case: For scripting when you need machine-readable output

options.description: Use the specified format instead of the default

common_misconceptions.title: stat shows file contents
common_misconceptions.misconception: stat displays the actual content of files
common_misconceptions.reality: stat only shows metadata (permissions, size, timestamps), not file contents. Use cat, less, or other commands to view file contents.
common_misconceptions.tip: Think of stat as 'file information' not 'file content'

common_misconceptions.title: Change time vs Modify time
common_misconceptions.misconception: Change time and modify time are the same
common_misconceptions.reality: Modify time changes when file content changes. Change time (ctime) changes when file metadata (permissions, ownership) changes. They can be different.
common_misconceptions.tip: Modify = content changed, Change = metadata changed

common_pitfalls.description: By default, stat shows information about the symlink itself, not the target
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -L flag to follow symlinks: stat -L symlink

common_pitfalls.description: Default output format is human-readable, not ideal for parsing
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -t for terse format or -c with format specifiers for machine-readable output

best_practices: Use -L when you need information about the target of a symlink
Use -c with format specifiers for scripting instead of parsing default output
Use -f to check file system information when debugging disk issues
Combine with find to check metadata of multiple files: find . -exec stat {} \;
performance_tips: For multiple files, stat is fast as it only reads metadata, not file contents
Use -t for faster output when you don't need human-readable format
Avoid stat on network file systems when possible as it requires network I/O

related_commands.relationship: Shows basic file information in directory listings
related_commands.description: ls -l provides similar but less detailed information than stat
file shows what type of file it is, while stat shows metadata

related_commands.relationship: Can use stat to filter files by metadata
related_commands.description: find -newer and similar options use stat information

additional_notes.note1: The 'Birth' time (file creation) is only available on certain file systems like ext4 with specific mount options
additional_notes.note2: On some systems, 'Change' time is called 'ctime' and refers to inode change time
additional_notes.note3: stat format specifiers (used with -c) include: %A (permissions), %n (name), %s (size), %U (user), %G (group), %y (modify time), and many more
